accuracy.evidence: Research claims checked against the papers: Pressley (1976, J. Educ. Psychol. 68, 355-359) trained 8-year-olds to form a mental image for each section of a story and they answered more short-answer questions than controls who read it; Gambrell and Bales (1986, Reading Research Quarterly 21, 454-464) found fourth- and fifth-grade poor readers (ages 9 to 11) told to form mental images detected more inconsistencies in a text; Hegarty and Kozhevnikov (1999, J. Educ. Psychol. 91, 684-689) found schematic imagery (spatial relations, how many) was linked to success in mathematical problem solving while pictorial imagery (how things look) was not. The EEF Metacognition and self-regulated learning guidance (2021) recommends explicitly teaching such strategies with modelling and practice. Maths answers checked at every corner: posts a-1 (a 3..7 gives 2..6), Ben a-2 (a 5..9 gives 3..7), lamp posts 5*(a-1) (a 2..6 gives 5..25), Mia a-3 (a 6..10 gives 3..7); lab problems 5 posts 2 m apart = 4 gaps = 8 m, Sam 4th of 10 has 6 behind, challenge 4 posts 5 m apart = 15 m.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: reading on without building a picture (Build step: every card placed from the words, the boat must exist before the cat can go on its roof); keeping the first picture when the text changes it (A new sentence predict 'Keep the cat on the boat roof', 3 sentences that move the cat, add 2 gulls and move the crab; p3, challenge 'keep'); not noticing that a picture does not fit (Does it fit? predict 'Keep reading and ignore it', 3 robot pictures with a wrong position, wrong number, wrong side; p5, m5, m8, challenge 'ignore'); pictorial rather than schematic pictures for maths (Picture a problem predict, 'Every flower and cloud' refused; m2, challenge 'fancy', after Hegarty and Kozhevnikov); counting posts instead of gaps (10 m and 5 m answers named; p2, m3, challenge 'posts'); adding details the words do not give (sorter card, challenge 'any').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagmindpic is about building a mental model from text: a harbour built card by card from a description, the same picture updated by three new sentences, a robot's street picture checked against the words (position, number, left/right), a posts-and-gaps and a line-of-children problem solved by picking and building a schematic picture, and a bedroom rebuilt from memory after hiding the words. No other flagship lab does text-to-scene placement with update, mismatch detection and recall; the lab_distinct gate measures it under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is discovered by doing: wrong places are refused with the sentence quoted back ('Not on the jetty. The new sentence says ...'), the cat cannot go on a roof before the boat exists, the mismatch tap names what the words say against what the picture shows, building 5 posts shows only 4 gaps appear before the 8 m answer is asked, tapping the 4th child turns the 6 behind green, and the room must be rebuilt with the words hidden (a Peek button is counted). Done messages confirm each rule after the task; the finished problem step shows both solved schematic pictures with their working.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option that the lab disproves: 'Keep the cat on the boat roof' (the next sentence moves it and the old picture no longer matches), 'Keep reading and ignore it' (each robot picture has a real error the words reveal), 'A detailed drawing of everything' (the flowers-and-clouds picture is refused as no help for counting) and 'Say the words over and over' (the words are hidden and only the picture remains). The correct option is first in one and second in three.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions; every wrong option is tagged and names the slip: any ('Your picture has to come from the words ... Do not add or move things the words do not say'), keep ('When a new sentence changes a detail, change your picture too'), ignore ('A picture that does not fit is a signal: stop, reread'), fancy ('Decorations do not help ... where things are and how many'), posts ('4 posts make only 3 gaps, and 3 gaps of 5 m is 15 m'), skip ('Picturing what you read helps you understand it and remember it'). In-lab feedback names the slip too: '10 m counts a gap for every post', '7 is 10 - 3, as if Sam were 3rd', 'The words say two balls, but the picture shows three'.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (picture, where, how many, change, reread, dots, gaps) with one idea each; the adult text names the age, key words, the three studies and the common mistakes plainly; validate_lessons readability passes for kid and adult text. Canvas texts are short story sentences an 8-year-old can read, and every action is announced through the live region.

no_filler.evidence: Every sentence teaches a move (picture the details, change it, check it, keep maths pictures simple, use it to remember) or gives evidence; no throat-clearing or template text; the content gate finds no filler phrase and under 12% overlap with every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 (390 px) screenshots in light and dark and on desktop 1280 px: the story text wraps in a box above the picture, the boat, cat, gulls (now drawn with head, wing and legs, standing on the post, roof and jetty rather than floating), crab, lamp, ball and clock sit on their surfaces, the four word cards and all buttons are full size, the posts and children pictures fit, and the finished problem step shows both solved pictures; nothing is clipped.

accessibility.evidence: Everything can be done with buttons as well as drag or tap: Pick up the boat/cat/gull/crab then Put it on the jetty / at the end of the jetty etc., a button for every picture part in Does it fit?, Every flower and cloud / Dots and gaps, Add a post, Child 3/4/5 from the front and the answer buttons, Hide the words / Peek at the words. The canvas aria-label is updated on every action (what moved where, what does not fit, the problem state, the challenge question); the walk gate's axe run finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark on desktop and phone.

sources: Pressley, G. M. (1976). Mental imagery helps eight-year-olds remember what they read. Journal of Educational Psychology, 68(3), 355-359
Gambrell, L. B., and Bales, R. J. (1986). Mental imagery and the comprehension-monitoring performance of fourth- and fifth-grade poor readers. Reading Research Quarterly, 21(4), 454-464
Hegarty, M., and Kozhevnikov, M. (1999). Types of visual-spatial representations and mathematical problem solving. Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(4), 684-689
